column4: The source section defines جهر as raising the voice against secrecy; this verse says even if speech is raised, God knows the secret and what is more hidden, completing the same audible-to-hidden span.
The source section's loud and inward reading becomes an explicit prayer boundary: do not تَجْهَر (raise the voice) or تَخَافَت (suppress it), but seek a way between them.
The section links remembrance to tongue and heart; this command places remembrance within oneself, in humility and fear, below loud speech.
The source's hidden side is enacted as prayer: call upon the Lord humbly and خُفْيَةً (secretly), not as public speech.
This verse directly pairs what God knows as الجهر من القول (open speech) with what people conceal, matching the section's governing claim.
This is the section's two sound states in one command: whether you conceal your speech or speak aloud, God knows what is within breasts.
The verse stages speech concealed or spoken aloud, then the person hidden by night or manifest by day; it makes the section's hidden/visible pair both vocal and bodily.
The section joins hiddenness to emergence through the source root خ ر ج; here God brings out الْخَبْءَ (the hidden thing) in heaven and earth and knows what people hide and reveal.
God is explicitly said to know the secret and the public, a direct formulation of the section's claim that both inner and voiced states are known.
People try to hide their words from other people at night, but cannot hide them from God; this sharpens the section's distinction between human concealment and divine knowledge.
The verse pictures people folding their breasts and covering themselves with garments to conceal, while God knows what they hide and disclose; it gives concealment a physical covering.
The verse states that God knows what people conceal and what they declare, directly echoing the section's paired hidden and manifest states.
Abraham says God knows what they hide and what they make manifest; this makes the section's hidden/open pair a prayer spoken in God's presence.
God says He knows what the angels disclose and what they had concealed; the scene gives the section's hidden/manifest pair a concrete disclosure.
This asks whether people know that God knows what they conceal and declare, directly extending the section's account of divine knowledge beyond audible speech.
The verse applies concealment and disclosure to what lies in people's breasts; it makes explicit that the section's inward side includes intention, not only quiet speech.
After the Messenger's duty to convey, the verse says God knows what people disclose and conceal, connecting public delivery with what remains hidden.
God knows what they conceal and disclose even when they are proud; this repeats the section's paired knowledge claim in a morally exposing context.
This says the Lord knows what people's breasts conceal and what they declare, making the section's inward/outward contrast explicit.
The verse says God knows what people conceal and disclose, extending the same paired claim to everything in heaven and earth.
God knows the stealth of eyes and what breasts conceal; this gives the section's hidden side a concrete, partly visible act that still escapes people.
Not even a falling leaf escapes God's knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of earth; the verse joins hidden growth under soil to the section's claim about what God knows.
This is an exact field parallel to 87:4: God brings out its water and pasture, using أَخْرَجَ for the emergence of الْمَرْعَىٰ.
Rain runs through the earth, crops emerge in varied colors, then yellow and become debris; the full cycle closely parallels the section's pasture emerging and passing away.
Water from heaven grows mixed vegetation, which dries and is scattered by winds; it gives the section's plant-emergence image its full impermanent arc.
Rain grows the land's produce, then it becomes cut down and debris as though it had not flourished; this is a close parallel to pasture emerging and becoming غُثَاءً.
The verse describes water driven to barren land and crops brought forth for people and their cattle, a direct version of pasture emerging after rain.
God sends water down and brings out vegetation, green growth, grain, and fruit; this gives a concrete instance of the section's earth yielding what was covered.
Winds drive a rain cloud to dead land, and water brings forth fruits there; the verse stages the section's movement from hidden earth to visible growth.
Rain is sent down from the sky and becomes drink and water for plants; it supplies the rain side of the section's emergence scene.
By that water God grows grain, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits; the verse spells out what comes forth from the rain in the section's image.
The verse asks who grows what people sow; it makes the section's emergence of pasture an act whose source belongs to God.
It answers that God is the one who causes the crop to grow, directly linking the section's raised-from-earth image to divine action.
God says He could make the crop dry fragments; this parallels the section's movement from green pasture to غُثَاءً.
The day when hidden secrets are tested or laid bare is a direct disclosure of what had remained concealed, the section's second scene at its final horizon.
The earth brings out its burdens; this is a specific emergence from concealment and echoes the source section's extraction root خ ر ج.
When the graves are overturned and their contents brought out, the verse turns the section's emergence from a covering into bodily disclosure.
What lies within breasts is brought to light; this joins the section's inner speech with the unearthing of concealed things.
A private statement between the Prophet and a wife is disclosed, and God informs him of it; the scene shows concealed speech becoming manifest under divine knowledge.
The source section names خ ف ي as concealment; in Moses' address, the coming Hour is said to be nearly concealed, giving concealment a divine limit.
The verse tells the Prophet not to move his tongue hastily with the recitation, making the tongue's physical role in the section's aloud/inner reading explicit.
God takes responsibility for the Qur'an's collection and recitation, directly meeting the section's account of being taught to recite.
When God recites the Qur'an, the Prophet is told to follow its recitation; this gives the section's reading scene an audible model and response.
God witnesses the Prophet's activity and whatever portion of Qur'an he recites; this directly joins the section's recitation in 87:6 to God's knowing in 87:7.
The Qur'an is recited in stages to strengthen the Prophet's heart; this connects the section's spoken recitation with its inward reception.
When God's name is mentioned hearts tremble, and recited verses increase faith; the verse shows spoken remembrance entering the inner state named in the section.
Recited revelation makes the skins of those who fear God shiver and then their hearts soften; it traces sound into inward response, joining the section's two locations of remembrance.
Nothing in earth or heaven is hidden from God; this states the section's hidden/known relation in the most direct terms.
God is knower of the unseen and does not disclose His unseen to anyone; this sets a boundary on the section's hidden-to-revealed movement.
This names the approved messenger as the exception to 72:26's withholding of the unseen; its own contribution is to show how hidden knowledge may be disclosed.

Moses is commanded to worship God and establish prayer for His remembrance; it gives the section's remembrance-then-prayer detail a parallel in the same address, before 20:15 turns to the concealed Hour.
The people who lower their voices before the Messenger are described as having hearts God has tested; following 49:2, this links outward sound to inward state.
This calls God knower of the unseen and witnessed; 13:10 then makes that distinction audible through secret or open speech, while this row supplies the divine frame.
The verse concerns what people disclose or conceal within themselves; it extends the source section's hidden state from remembered words to inward accountability.
The verse says God knows the hypocrites' secret talk and private counsel, a concrete hidden-speech case within the section's claim.
Private conversations cannot be hidden from God, who is with their participants and will inform them of their deeds; this extends the section's hidden-speech scene to a group.
The people thought they could conceal their acts, but their hearing, eyes, and skins testify; this is a boundary on what concealment can protect.
God is invoked as knower of the unseen and the witnessed; this gives the section's hidden/manifest pair a concise epistemic formulation.
God knows the unseen in heaven and earth and what breasts contain; the verse carries the section's inward knowledge claim into creation's unseen.
Asked who sends water and gives life to dead earth, the people answer God; it states the rain-to-emergence relation underlying the section's pasture image.
The verse describes rain sent down and fruits brought forth from the earth as provision, a direct though general instance of emergence.
Rain from heaven gives life to earth after its death; it makes the section's emerging pasture a sign of hidden life becoming visible.
God sends water down and brings forth fruits as provision; it connects the section's extraction image to divine provision.
God spreads the earth, sends down water, and produces varied kinds of plants; it parallels the section's pasture emerging from earth.
Rain makes the dead earth stir and swell, then grow every beautiful kind; this supplies a detailed soil-to-growth scene for the section's emergence.
Water is sent down in measure and settled in the earth; it gives the section's pasture emergence its water stored beneath the surface.
The next verse brings forth gardens, dates, and grapes from that water; its own contribution is the visible yield that follows 23:18.
The olive tree growing from Mount Sinai and producing oil is another specific plant emerging from its place.
Rain revives the earth after its death; the verse makes the section's emergence-from-earth image a sign of God's power.
God sends winds that raise clouds and spread them; this supplies the cloud stage before the rain and growth paired with the section's pasture.
The rain cloud brings glad tidings before water descends; following 30:48, this row contributes the arrival of rain that enables emergence.
The verse directs attention to God's mercy in giving life to earth after death; it completes the rain sequence of 30:48-49 with the visible result.
Winds drive clouds to dead land and God gives life to earth after death; this is a concrete cloud-to-emergence scene.
Dead earth comes alive and yields grain; this is a close crop-and-earth instance of what the section says emerges.
The following verse supplies date gardens and grapevines; its own contribution is the fruit-bearing growth from revived land.
The next verse names the fruit people eat; it completes 36:33-34 by showing the yield of the emerging gardens.
Barren earth stirs when water descends and grows; this is a close, observable version of the section's covered ground yielding vegetation.
Water is sent down in due measure to revive dead land; it links the section's rain-fed emergence with divine measure.
Blessed rain grows gardens, grain, and harvest; it is a direct agricultural parallel to the pasture brought out in 87:4.
The next verse names tall date palms with clustered fruit; its own contribution is a specific visible yield from the growth introduced in 50:9.
This verse calls the crops provision and says dead land is revived; it completes 50:9-10 with the purpose and result of growth.
Rain-fed growth delights people, then dries and becomes debris; it parallels the section's pasture and its passing into withered remains.
The section describes pasture emerging from earth; this verse uses plant-growth language for human beings, extending the image from vegetation to living forms.
Abundant rain is sent down from clouds; 78:15 names the grain and vegetation it brings forth, so this row supplies the water stage.
The verse says rain brings out grain and vegetation; its own contribution is the crop emerging from the water in 78:14.
This verse's gardens complete 78:14-15's rain-to-crop sequence with a cultivated visible yield.
Water is poured down abundantly, beginning a sequence in which the earth opens and crops emerge, paralleling the section's rain-fed pasture.
The earth is split open after the rain of 80:25; its own contribution is the opening ground from which the listed crops emerge.
Grain is the first growth named after the earth splits in 80:26; it makes emergence tangible.
The following crop is grapes; its own contribution is another specific fruit of the opened earth.
Olives and palms follow in the crop sequence; the verse adds named trees to what emerges from the earth.
Dense gardens follow the listed crops; this verse contributes the larger growth that emerges from the ground.
The verse names fruit and pasture, including أَبًّا (fodder), closely matching the section's pasture image.
The final verse calls these yields provision for people and livestock; it completes the scene of growth begun in 80:25.
The section connects recitation to sound; the command to recite the Qur'an in measured recitation makes its vocal shaping explicit.
The Qur'an of dawn is specifically named as recitation and described as witnessed, adding a public, heard setting to the section's reciting.
The verse links remembrance of God with hearts becoming tranquil; it gives the section's inward side of ذكر a concrete result.
These people remember God in every posture and reflect inwardly on creation; it extends the section's remembrance from the tongue to sustained inner attention.
Daylight makes what was covered visible; this natural visibility/covering pair mirrors the section's transition from concealed to apparent.
The verse describes a plant sending out its shoot and strengthening into a firm stem; it extends the section's emergence image from first appearance to growth.
The section's source root ج ه ر means raised speech; this verse sets a boundary on الْجَهْرَ بِالسُّوءِ, permitting public evil speech only from one who has been wronged.
The verse forbids raising voices above the Prophet's voice, a concrete limit on vocal elevation that gives the section's loud side a social boundary.
The command وَاغْضُضْ مِن صَوْتِكَ (lower your voice) makes measured vocal volume a practical boundary, complementing the section's loud/inward axis.
The source's dictionary note says a جَهْرَاء eye may fail in sunlight; here the eye is dazzled, showing that excessive brightness can itself defeat seeing.
Lightning nearly snatches away sight; this gives the section's note that too much light can act as a veil a literal Qur'anic image.
In the parable, lightning briefly illuminates the way but nearly takes their sight; it shows the boundary noted in the source dictionary, where excess light can veil.
The verse commands leaving both apparent and inward sin; it makes the section's visible/hidden boundary a moral distinction rather than a sound distinction.
God forbids indecency both apparent and hidden; it applies the section's paired states to conduct that may be exposed or covered.
After the dazzled eye in 75:7, the moon is darkened; this contributes the loss-of-light side of the same vision boundary.
Night covers what daylight displays in 91:3; it gives the section's visible/hidden boundary a natural reversal.
Zakariya calls his Lord with a hidden call; this directly joins the source section's خ ف ي root to speech made inward and private.
God has heard the woman disputing with the Prophet and complaining to God; this makes divine knowledge of voiced speech a concrete scene.
The verse asks whether people think God does not hear their secrets and private conversations, directly joining hidden speech to divine awareness.
The hypocrites fear a surah will disclose what is in their hearts; this joins the section's recited word with what was concealed inside.
In the murder story, God brings out what the people had concealed; the verse directly combines the source section's extraction root خ ر ج with hidden matter becoming manifest.
Satan whispers to Adam and Eve in order to expose what had been covered of their nakedness; this joins hidden speech to the transition from covered to visible.
After they eat, their nakedness becomes manifest and they cover themselves with leaves; the verse stages disclosure followed by a renewed covering.
The verse says fruit emerges from its coverings and God knows what each female carries and gives birth to; it directly joins emergence from cover with divine knowledge.
God splits grain and date stones and brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living; this links plant emergence with the source section's extraction root.
God brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living, revives earth after its death, and brings people forth; this makes the source's emergence from place or state explicit.
A Messenger recites God's clear signs to bring believers from darkness into light; it joins audible revelation with the source root's emergence from a state.
God brings believers out of darkness into light; the source section's root خ ر ج is defined as emerging from a place or state, and this verse makes the state change explicit.
The verse bars prayer until a person knows what they are saying; it makes awareness of spoken prayer explicit, echoing the source section's explanation of علم as noticing or perceiving.
This verse places recitation beside prayer and remembrance of God, bringing together the section's reading in 87:6 and remembrance followed by prayer in 87:15.
The hypocrites say with their mouths what is not in their hearts; this reverses the section's joined tongue-and-heart remembrance and shows why God knowing both matters.
The Bedouins' tongues say what their hearts do not contain; this is another specific case where voiced speech and hidden inward state diverge.
God knows the soul's whisper; this gives the section's inward or silent speech a direct Qur'anic counterpart.
Every word uttered is watched and recorded; following 50:17's two recorders, this verse contributes the accountability of spoken words.
In danger at sea or land, people call on God humbly and خُفْيَةً (secretly); it is a concrete hidden-prayer scene.
The verse says God taught the human being البيان, articulated expression; it connects to the source section's account of speech and the physical shaping of voiced letters.
The hypocrites answer that they were only talking and playing; following 9:64's fear that revelation will expose their hearts, this verse supplies their spoken excuse.
People continue private conversations about sin, hostility, and disobedience; this extends 58:7's scene of speech that cannot be hidden from God.
Believers are told not to confer privately about sin or disobedience but about righteousness and piety; following 58:8, this sets a moral boundary on hidden speech.
The next verse says private conversation can be used by Satan to grieve believers; its own contribution is the harm a hidden exchange can carry.
On the day people emerge before God, nothing about them is hidden from Him; it joins coming out into view with the section's claim about the hidden.
God brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living; this applies the source section's root خ ر ج to a change of state.
In answer to who governs provision and life, the verse says God brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living; it repeats the source root's state-change sense.
The Book is sent to bring people from darkness into light; this uses the source root's emergence-from-a-state sense for revelation.
Moses is sent to bring his people out of darkness into light; it repeats the source section's state-change meaning in a prophetic mission.
The Book guides to paths of peace and brings people from darkness into light; it links revealed guidance to the source root's emergence from a state.
God brings believers out of darkness into light; this is another direct Qur'anic use of emergence as a change of state.
God sends clear signs to bring believers out of darkness into light, joining revelation and the source section's emergence image.

A person who was dead is given life and a light by which to walk among people, in contrast with one remaining in darkness; it gives the section's emergence-from-a-state image a concrete transformation.
Pearls and coral emerge from the seas; this is a specific example of something coming out from a place, matching the source section's extraction sense.
People call to the Prophet from outside his private chambers; it gives the section's loud-speech side a concrete public-call scene.
The verse says it would be better for them to wait until the Prophet comes out; following 49:4's calls from outside, it supplies the contrasting restraint.
